QF.id: AIFM CII Investment Process and Governance_23

question.text: A Shareholders' Agreement (SHA) is typically required alongside the SSA because:

answer.text: The SHA is signed only by the AIF and the investment banker
The SSA binds only the company, not the existing shareholders; the SHA binds existing shareholders to the agreed rights and obligations
SEBI regulations mandate a separate SHA for every AIF investment
The SHA replaces the Articles of Association entirely

explanation.text: The Logic: Per the workbook (pages 225-226), the SSA is between the company and the AIF, so the SSA conditions bind the company but do not bind shareholders that are not party to it. The SHA is the inter-se agreement among the existing shareholders that binds them to the new rights and obligations (such as tag-along, drag-along, ROFR, and affirmative rights). Per pages 232-233, the Articles of Association are amended to incorporate the relevant SHA provisions. The Trap: SEBI does not mandate the SHA for every AIF investment. The SHA does not replace the AOA; rather, the AOA is amended to mirror the SHA. The investment banker is not a party to the SHA. Note: Amending the AOA to incorporate SHA-protected provisions (particularly tag-along, drag-along, and affirmative rights) is an important step. Without an AOA amendment, the interaction between SHA rights and company law remedies should be reviewed on a case-by-case basis.
